quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.title: Path Integral for the Wave Function of the Universe

\\Psi.name: Wave function of the Universe
\\Psi.description: A functional that assigns a complex probability amplitude to a given 3-geometry and matter field configuration on a spatial hypersurface.

a.name: Scale factor
a.description: A parameter that describes the relative expansion of the universe, often used as a coordinate in simplified minisuperspace models.

\\phi.name: Matter fields
\\phi.description: A collective representation of all matter and energy fields (e.g., scalar fields) within the spacetime.

\\int\\mathcal{D}g\\mathcal{D}\\phi.name: Path Integral Operator
\\int\\mathcal{D}g\\mathcal{D}\\phi.description: A functional integral over the space of all possible spacetime metrics ($g$) and matter field configurations ($\phi$).

g.name: Spacetime metric tensor
g.description: The dynamical field of general relativity that defines the geometry of spacetime.

S.name: Action
S.description: The total action for the system, typically the Einstein-Hilbert action for gravity plus the action for all matter fields.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck constant
\\hbar.description: The fundamental constant of quantum mechanics, linking energy to frequency.

quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.interpretation: In this equation, $\Psi[a, \phi]$ is the wave function of the universe. It is a functional of the universe's 3-geometry, often simplified in minisuperspace models to be a function of the scale factor, $a$, and the configuration of matter fields, denoted by $\phi$, on that 3-dimensional spatial slice. The integral $\int \mathcal{D}g \mathcal{D}\phi$ signifies a functional path integral over all possible 4-dimensional spacetime geometries, parameterized by the metric tensor $g$, and all possible configurations of the matter fields $\phi$. The term $e^{iS/\hbar}$ is the complex phase factor, where $S$ is the classical action of the universe (typically the Einstein-Hilbert action plus a matter action), and $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant. This exponential term assigns a complex amplitude to each possible history of the universe, embodying the principle of superposition in quantum mechanics applied to the entire cosmos.
quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.symmetry_origin: The formulation is fundamentally based on general covariance (diffeomorphism invariance), the core gauge symmetry of General Relativity, which dictates that the laws of physics are the same for all observers in arbitrary relative motion. The path integral measure must be constructed to respect this invariance.
quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit, as the reduced Planck constant $\hbar \to 0$, the method of stationary phase dictates that the path integral is dominated by the single history for which the action $S$ is stationary. This recovers the classical equations of motion (Einstein's field equations) from the quantum framework. The definition of $\Psi$ is highly dependent on the boundary conditions imposed on the path integral, with different choices (e.g., the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal or Vilenkin's tunneling proposal) leading to different theories of cosmic initial conditions.
quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.conceptual_definition: The wave function of the universe, $\Psi$, which assigns a quantum amplitude to a specific spatial geometry and matter configuration, is computed by summing over all possible four-dimensional spacetime histories that result in that configuration. Each history is weighted by a phase factor, $e^{iS/\hbar}$, determined by its total classical action, $S$.
quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.intuitive_summary: Imagine the universe's quantum state not as a single reality, but as a superposition of all possible universes that could exist. This formula is the mathematical recipe for adding up all those possibilities, where each potential universe's contribution is weighted by a value derived from its entire life story (its 'action'). The result is the 'wave function of the universe,' which tells us which cosmic configurations are most probable.
quantum-cosmology-291b3c03.description: A foundational formula in quantum cosmology that defines the wave function of the universe as a Feynman path integral over all possible spacetime geometries and matter field configurations.

time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.title: Time Reversal Transformation for Time and Momentum
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.interpretation: The expression $t \to -t$ signifies a transformation where the time coordinate, $t$ (measured in seconds, $\text{s}$), is replaced by its negative. This represents the reversal of the direction of time's flow. The expression $\mathbf{p} \to -\mathbf{p}$ represents the transformation of the momentum vector, $\mathbf{p}$ (measured in kilogram-meters per second, $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}/\text{s}$). Replacing $\mathbf{p}$ with $-\mathbf{p}$ means that the direction of momentum is reversed, while its magnitude remains unchanged. For a physical system to exhibit time reversal symmetry, its governing equations must remain invariant under these simultaneous transformations of $t$ and $\mathbf{p}$.
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.symmetry_origin: Time reversal symmetry is a discrete spacetime symmetry, often associated with the invariance of physical laws under the reversal of motion. While not directly linked to a Noether conservation law in the same way as continuous symmetries, its violation (CPT theorem) has profound implications for fundamental interactions.
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.limits_and_boundary: In classical mechanics, time reversal symmetry generally holds for systems governed by conservative forces, where friction or other dissipative forces are absent. In quantum mechanics, the time reversal operator $\mathcal{T}$ is anti-unitary and anti-linear; its application to a state $|\psi(t)\rangle$ yields $\mathcal{T}|\psi(t)\rangle = |\psi(-t)\rangle$. The weak nuclear force is known to violate time reversal symmetry (T-violation), which is linked to CP-violation by the CPT theorem. For systems with magnetic fields, the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ must also reverse direction under time reversal, i.e., $\mathbf{B} \to -\mathbf{B}$, because it arises from moving charges.
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.conceptual_definition: Time reversal symmetry implies that the laws of physics remain invariant under the transformation where the time coordinate $t$ is replaced by $-t$, and the momentum $\mathbf{p}$ is replaced by $-\mathbf{p}$. This transformation effectively reverses the direction of motion for all particles in a system.
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.intuitive_summary: Imagine playing a movie backward: time runs in reverse, and everything that was moving forward now moves backward. This formula describes how time itself and the 'oomph' (momentum) of objects change in that backward-running movie.
time-reversal-symmetry-c740ca81.description: This formula defines the fundamental transformations of time and momentum under a time reversal operation, where the direction of time's flow is inverted, and consequently, the direction of momentum is also inverted.

stability-limit-bf4019ee.title: Radiative Acceleration

f_{rad}.name: Radiative Acceleration
f_{rad}.description: The acceleration imparted to a unit mass of material by the momentum flux of a radiation field.

\\kappa.name: Opacity
\\kappa.description: A measure of a material's capacity to absorb and scatter radiation per unit mass.

L.name: Luminosity
L.description: The total energy radiated by the source per unit time.

r.name: Radial Distance
r.description: The distance from the center of the radiating source.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The universal speed of light, a fundamental physical constant.

stability-limit-bf4019ee.interpretation: The formula $f_{rad} = \frac{\kappa L}{4\pi r^2 c}$ quantifies the radiative acceleration, which is the force per unit mass exerted by radiation. This is a critical component in the study of stellar structure and stability. The term $\frac{L}{4\pi r^2}$ represents the energy flux at a distance $r$. Dividing this by the speed of light $c$ gives the momentum flux of the radiation field. The opacity $\kappa$ is a measure of the material's ability to absorb or scatter photons; a higher opacity means more momentum is transferred from the radiation field to the matter, resulting in a larger acceleration $f_{rad}$. The entire expression shows that the radiative acceleration increases with the star's energy output ($L$) and the material's opacity ($\kappa$), and decreases with the square of the distance ($r$) due to the geometric dilution of the radiation field.
stability-limit-bf4019ee.symmetry_origin: Derived from the conservation of momentum in photon-matter interactions, assuming isotropic emission from a central source, which imposes spherical symmetry on the resulting radiation field.
stability-limit-bf4019ee.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of large distance, as $r \to \infty$, the radiative acceleration $f_{rad} \to 0$. If the material is perfectly transparent, $\kappa \to 0$, then $f_{rad} \to 0$ as no momentum is transferred. Similarly, if the source has no luminosity, $L \to 0$, then $f_{rad} \to 0$. The formula is a classical approximation and does not account for general relativistic effects.
stability-limit-bf4019ee.conceptual_definition: Radiative acceleration, denoted as $f_{rad}$, is the force per unit mass exerted by a radiation field on matter. It is directly proportional to the luminosity $L$ of the source and the opacity $\kappa$ of the material, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance $r$ from the source. This relationship arises from the momentum carried by photons, which is transferred to the material upon absorption or scattering.
stability-limit-bf4019ee.intuitive_summary: Imagine a star as a giant light bulb. The light it emits pushes outwards on the gas that makes up the star. This push, or acceleration, is stronger closer to the core and for gas that is better at blocking light (higher opacity). The formula calculates how strong this outward push is on any given piece of stellar material.
stability-limit-bf4019ee.description: Defines the outward acceleration experienced by a unit mass of material due to the momentum transfer from radiation (photons) originating from a central source.

non-local-links-6fef8adc.title: Von Neumann Entropy of a Quantum System

S.name: von Neumann entropy
S.description: Total quantum statistical mechanical entropy of the state

\\rho.name: density matrix
\\rho.description: Positive semi-definite Hermitian density operator describing the quantum ensemble

\\text{Tr}.name: trace operator
\\text{Tr}.description: Sum of the diagonal matrix elements or spectral eigenvalues

non-local-links-6fef8adc.interpretation: In this formula, $S$ denotes the von Neumann entropy with SI units of Joules per Kelvin ($\text{J/K}$), scaled by Boltzmann's constant $k_B$. The density operator $\rho$ is a positive semi-definite trace-class operator on the system Hilbert space satisfying $\text{Tr}(\rho) = 1$. The functional $\text{Tr}(\rho \ln \rho)$ represents the trace of the matrix logarithm operator $\rho \ln \rho$, which in the eigenbasis $\rho = \sum_i p_i |\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|$ reduces to the Shannon-like sum $\sum_i p_i \ln p_i$.
non-local-links-6fef8adc.symmetry_origin: Invariance under unitary transformations $\rho \to U \rho U^\dagger$ due to the cyclic property of the trace, establishing conservation of entropy under closed unitary quantum time evolution.
non-local-links-6fef8adc.limits_and_boundary: For a pure state $\rho = |\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$, $S = 0$. For a maximally mixed state in a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space $\rho = \frac{1}{d}\mathbb{I}$, the entropy reaches its upper bound $S = k_B \ln d$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, $S$ converges to the classical Gibbs entropy.
non-local-links-6fef8adc.conceptual_definition: The von Neumann entropy extends classical Gibbs-Shannon entropy to quantum statistical mechanics via the spectral decomposition of the density matrix $\rho$. It is defined as $S = -k_B \text{Tr}(\rho \ln \rho)$, measuring both classical statistical ignorance in mixed ensembles and quantum bipartite entanglement entropy when restricted to reduced subsystems.
non-local-links-6fef8adc.intuitive_summary: Measures the degree of classical ignorance or quantum mixing in a quantum state: it evaluates to zero for pure states and reaches a maximum for uniformly mixed statistical ensembles.
non-local-links-6fef8adc.description: Fundamental quantum generalization of thermodynamic Gibbs-Boltzmann entropy, quantifying the statistical mixture and missing information of a quantum state represented by a density operator.

field-strength-law-8eebab9b.title: Field Strength Law

u_B.name: Magnetic Energy Density
u_B.description: The potential energy stored per unit volume in a magnetic field. It represents how concentrated the magnetic energy is in space.

B.name: Magnetic Field Strength
B.description: The magnitude of the magnetic field vector, also known as magnetic flux density. It quantifies the strength of the magnetic field at a given point in space.

\\mu_0.name: Permeability of Free Space
\\mu_0.description: A fundamental physical constant that represents the ability of a vacuum to permit magnetic field lines. It is a measure of how easily a magnetic field can be established in a vacuum.

u.name: Velocity Component / Specific Internal Energy
u.description: Speed along a particular coordinate direction, or internal energy per unit mass.

field-strength-law-8eebab9b.interpretation: This equation, $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$, relates the energy density of a magnetic field to the magnetic field strength itself. The term $u_B$ represents the magnetic energy density, measured in Joules per cubic meter (J/m³), which is the amount of potential energy stored per unit volume of space due to the presence of the magnetic field. The variable $B$ is the magnitude of the magnetic field vector, measured in Teslas ( $T$). It is squared in the equation, indicating that the energy density increases quadratically with the magnetic field strength; doubling the magnetic field quadruples the stored energy density. The constant $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, approximately $4π \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}·\text{m/A}$. It is a fundamental constant that describes how easily magnetic field lines can permeate a vacuum. Its presence in the denominator signifies that a medium with higher permeability can support a stronger magnetic field for the same energy density, or conversely, store more energy for a given field strength.
field-strength-law-8eebab9b.symmetry_origin: The Field Strength Law for magnetic energy density can be derived from the Poynting theorem, which describes the flow of electromagnetic energy. Specifically, it arises from considering the work done by the magnetic force on moving charges, which contributes to the energy stored in the field. In a more fundamental derivation, it can be obtained from the Lagrangian density for the electromagnetic field in a vacuum. The energy density is a scalar quantity and is invariant under Lorentz transformations, reflecting the relativistic nature of electromagnetism and the fact that energy and momentum are intertwined components of the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor.
field-strength-law-8eebab9b.limits_and_boundary: As the magnetic field strength $B$ approaches zero (i.e., $B \to 0$), the magnetic energy density $u_B$ also approaches zero ($u_B \to 0$). This is consistent with the physical intuition that in the absence of a magnetic field, there is no energy stored within it. Conversely, as the magnetic field strength $B$ tends towards infinity ($B \to ∞$), the magnetic energy density $u_B$ also tends towards infinity ($u_B \to ∞$). This indicates that magnetic fields can store an arbitrarily large amount of energy, provided that the materials involved can sustain such field strengths without saturating or undergoing breakdown.
field-strength-law-8eebab9b.conceptual_definition: The Field Strength Law, given by the equation $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$, quantifies the energy density stored within a magnetic field. It states that the energy per unit volume is directly proportional to the square of the magnetic field strength and inversely proportional to the permeability of free space. This formula is fundamental in electromagnetism, as it describes how magnetic fields, which are generated by electric currents or magnetic materials, contain and distribute energy throughout space.
field-strength-law-8eebab9b.intuitive_summary: The energy stored in a magnetic field is proportional to the square of its strength.

acceleration-effect-c89fffcb.interpretation:
In this equation, $A^μ$ represents the electromagnetic four-potential, a relativistic construct that combines the scalar electric potential $Φ$ and the vector magnetic potential $\textbf{A}$ into a single four-vector: $A^μ = ( \frac{1}{c} Φ, \textbf{A})$. The term $□$ is the d'Alembertian operator, defined as $□ = \nabla^2 - \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{∂^2}{∂ t^2} , where$
\nabla^2 is the Laplacian operator and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. This operator acts on the four-potential, indicating how it changes in spacetime. On the right-hand side, $j^μ is the electromagnetic four-current, which combines the charge density \rho and the current density \textbf {J}$into a four-vector:$j^μ = (c \rho , \textbf{J})$. This term represents the sources of the electromagnetic field. The constant$μ_0$ is the vacuum permeability, a fundamental constant of electromagnetism. The equation states that the spacetime variation of the electromagnetic four-potential is directly proportional to the density and flow of electric charge and current. In simpler terms, the distribution and movement of charges create the electromagnetic fields, and this equation governs how these fields behave and propagate as waves, such as light.
acceleration-effect-c89fffcb.symmetry_origin: This equation arises from Maxwell's equations in vacuum, specifically when assuming the Lorenz gauge condition ($\nabla · \textbf{A} + \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{∂ Φ}{∂ t} = 0$). When Maxwell's equations are rewritten in terms of the four-potential, and this gauge is applied, they reduce to two independent wave equations for the components of the four-potential. This form highlights the relativistic covariance of electromagnetism, as the four-potential and four-current are four-vectors, and the d'Alembertian operator is a Lorentz scalar.
acceleration-effect-c89fffcb.limits_and_boundary: In the static limit, where there are no time-varying fields or currents, the time derivative terms in the d'Alembertian operator become zero, simplifying the equation considerably. If we consider a situation with no currents ($j^μ = 0$), the equation becomes homogeneous, $□ A^μ = 0$, which describes the propagation of electromagnetic waves in the absence of sources. In the infinite limit for the magnitude of the four-current, the four-potential would also become infinitely large, indicating that sources are responsible for generating the fields. Conversely, if the four-current approaches zero, the four-potential also approaches zero (in the absence of pre-existing fields), implying that charge and current are the ultimate sources of electromagnetic phenomena.
acceleration-effect-c89fffcb.conceptual_definition: The given equation, □ A^μ = μ_0 j^μ, is a form of the wave equation in the context of electromagnetism. It describes how the electromagnetic four-potential, represented by the four-vector $A^μ$, is generated by the electromagnetic four-current, $j^μ$. The operator □ (the d'Alembertian operator) acts on the four-potential, and the proportionality constant is the vacuum permeability, $μ_0$. This equation is fundamental in establishing the relationship between sources (charge and current distributions) and the fields they produce, propagating as waves.
acceleration-effect-c89fffcb.intuitive_summary: The presence of electric charges and currents sources the disturbance in the electromagnetic potential, which then propagates as a wave.

flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.title: Matter Density Parameter Evolution

\\Omega_m(z).name: Matter Density Parameter at Redshift z
\\Omega_m(z).description: The ratio of the energy density of non-relativistic matter at redshift z to the critical density at that same redshift.

\\Omega_{m,0}.name: Matter Density Parameter Today
\\Omega_{m,0}.description: The present-day (z=0) fractional contribution of non-relativistic matter to the total energy density of the universe, relative to the critical density.

z.name: Redshift
z.description: A measure of the cosmic scale factor, related by $1+z = a_0/a$, indicating the amount of cosmic expansion since light was emitted.

E(z).name: Normalized Hubble Parameter
E(z).description: The ratio of the Hubble parameter $H(z)$ at redshift $z$ to the Hubble constant $H_0$, defined as $E(z) = H(z)/H_0$. Its square, $E^2(z)$, is proportional to the total energy density of the universe at redshift $z$.

flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.interpretation: This equation expresses the matter density parameter $\Omega_m(z)$ at a given redshift $z$. The numerator, $\Omega_{m,0}(1+z)^3$, shows how the density of non-relativistic matter scales with cosmic expansion; since volume scales as $a^3 \propto (1+z)^{-3}$, the density scales as $(1+z)^3$. The denominator, $E^2(z) = (H(z)/H_0)^2$, represents the total normalized energy density of the universe at that redshift. For a standard $\Lambda$CDM model, $E^2(z) = \Omega_{r,0}(1+z)^4 + \Omega_{m,0}(1+z)^3 + \Omega_{k,0}(1+z)^2 + \Omega_{\Lambda,0}$, where the terms represent radiation, matter, curvature, and dark energy, respectively. Therefore, $\Omega_m(z)$ gives the fraction of the total cosmic energy density that is in the form of matter at any epoch $z$.
flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.symmetry_origin: The formula is a direct consequence of the first Friedmann equation, which itself arises from applying Einstein's field equations of general relativity to a spacetime metric that respects the Cosmological Principle. This principle asserts that the universe is homogeneous and isotropic on large scales, a fundamental spacetime symmetry described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric. The evolution of each density component ($\Omega_i$) is governed by its corresponding equation of state, which is a phenomenological input.
flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.limits_and_boundary: 1. Present Day ($z \to 0$): The equation correctly recovers the present-day matter density parameter, as $\Omega_m(0) = \Omega_{m,0}(1+0)^3 / E^2(0) = \Omega_{m,0}$, since by definition $E(0)=1$. 2. Matter-Dominated Era ($z \gg 1$, before dark energy dominance): In an era where matter is the dominant energy component, $E^2(z) \approx \Omega_{m,0}(1+z)^3$, causing $\Omega_m(z)$ to approach 1. 3. Radiation-Dominated Era ($z \to \infty$): In the very early universe, radiation dominates, so $E^2(z) \approx \Omega_{r,0}(1+z)^4$. In this limit, $\Omega_m(z) \approx \frac{\Omega_{m,0}(1+z)^3}{\Omega_{r,0}(1+z)^4} = \frac{\Omega_{m,0}}{\Omega_{r,0}(1+z)}$, which approaches 0 as $z \to \infty$.
flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.conceptual_definition: The matter density parameter quantifies the contribution of non-relativistic matter (baryonic and dark) to the total energy density of the universe at a given redshift, expressed as a fraction of the critical density. It is a key parameter in the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) model, describing how the matter content influences cosmic expansion and geometry over time.
flatness-marker-bfa74ce4.intuitive_summary: This formula tracks the fraction of the universe's total energy density that is composed of matter as the universe expands through cosmic time.

the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.interpretation: In this equation, $\hat{ho}_B$ is the reduced density matrix of subsystem B, which describes the quantum state and statistical properties of subsystem B. The symbol $\text{Tr}_A$ denotes the partial trace operation over subsystem A, which mathematically 'integrates out' or 'averages over' the degrees of freedom associated with subsystem A. The term $|\Psiangle\langle\Psi|_{AB}$ represents the density matrix of the composite quantum system AB, which is formed from the outer product of the state vector $|\Psiangle_{AB}$ with itself. If the composite system AB is in a pure state, its state vector $|\Psiangle_{AB}$ can be expressed as a superposition in a product basis of A and B, such as $|\Psiangle_{AB} = \sum_{i,j} c_{ij} | a_i angle_A | b_j angle_B$, where $|a_iangle_A$ are basis vectors for subsystem A, $|b_jangle_B$ are basis vectors for subsystem B, and $c_{ij}$ are complex amplitude coefficients. The partial trace over A is formally defined as $\text{Tr}_A(\hat{O}_{AB}) = \sum_k \langle a_k |_A \hat{O}_{AB} | a_k angle_A$, where $\hat{O}_{AB}$ is an operator on the composite system and the sum is over a complete orthonormal basis $\{|a_kangle_A\}$ for subsystem A. This operation yields the statistical properties of subsystem B alone, which may be a mixed state even if the total system AB was in a pure state, a key concept in quantum entanglement.
the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.symmetry_origin: This formula is a mathematical definition for obtaining a reduced description of a quantum system, rather than being directly derived from a fundamental symmetry principle. However, the properties of the reduced density matrix are crucial for understanding symmetries related to entanglement and information conservation.
the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.limits_and_boundary: If subsystems A and B are unentangled, meaning the composite state can be written as a product state $|\Psiangle_{AB} = |\psiangle_A \otimes |\phiangle_B$, then the reduced density matrix for B simplifies to $\hat{ho}_B = |\phiangle\langle\phi|_B$, which is a pure state. If the composite system is already a mixed state, the partial trace operation still applies, yielding the reduced density matrix for the subsystem. The operation is always well-defined for any finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.conceptual_definition: The reduced density matrix $\hat{ho}_B$ of a subsystem $B$ is obtained by tracing out the degrees of freedom of the complementary subsystem $A$ from the density matrix of the composite system $AB$. This operation effectively describes the state of subsystem $B$ alone, even if $A$ and $B$ are entangled.
the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.intuitive_summary: Imagine you have two entangled particles, A and B. If you only care about particle B and want to describe its state without knowing anything about particle A, you 'forget' about A by averaging over all its possible states. This 'forgetting' process is the partial trace, and the resulting description for B is its reduced density matrix.
the-ftl-block-33c4d8ec.description: This formula defines the reduced density matrix of a subsystem by performing a partial trace over the degrees of freedom of the other subsystem in a composite quantum system. It is a fundamental operation in quantum information theory and the study of entanglement.

geometric-bending-08111f55.title: Boundary Condition for the Tangential Magnetic Field Intensity

\\mathbf{n}.name: Unit Normal Vector
\\mathbf{n}.description: Unit vector normal to the interface, pointing from medium 2 to medium 1.

\\mathbf{H}_1.name: Magnetic Field Intensity (Medium 1)
\\mathbf{H}_1.description: The magnetic field intensity vector in medium 1 at the boundary.

\\mathbf{H}_2.name: Magnetic Field Intensity (Medium 2)
\\mathbf{H}_2.description: The magnetic field intensity vector in medium 2 at the boundary.

\\mathbf{K}.name: Surface Current Density
\\mathbf{K}.description: The free electric current per unit length flowing on the surface interface.

\\times.name: Cross Product
\\times.description: A binary operation on two vectors in three-dimensional space.

geometric-bending-08111f55.interpretation: The equation $\mathbf{n} \times (\mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_2) = \mathbf{K}$ quantifies the behavior of the magnetic field intensity vector at an interface. Here, $\mathbf{H}_1$ is the magnetic field intensity in medium 1 and $\mathbf{H}_2$ is the magnetic field intensity in medium 2, both evaluated infinitesimally close to the boundary. The vector $\mathbf{n}$ is the unit normal vector pointing from medium 2 into medium 1. The cross product with $\mathbf{n}$ isolates the component of the magnetic field difference, $(\mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_2)$, that is tangential to the boundary. This tangential component is discontinuous if and only if a free surface current density, $\mathbf{K}$, exists on the boundary. $\mathbf{K}$ represents the flow of free charge per unit length perpendicular to the flow, with units of Amperes per meter (A/m). This boundary condition is a direct consequence of Ampere's Law.
geometric-bending-08111f55.symmetry_origin: Derived from Ampere's Law, which is a consequence of the U(1) gauge symmetry of electromagnetism. This symmetry implies the conservation of electric charge, and its local form dictates how currents (moving charges) act as sources for the magnetic field.
geometric-bending-08111f55.limits_and_boundary: In the absence of a free surface current, $\mathbf{K} = 0$, the equation simplifies to $\mathbf{n} \times (\mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_2) = 0$. This implies that the tangential component of the magnetic field intensity $\mathbf{H}$ is continuous across the boundary. This is the case for most dielectric interfaces. A non-zero $\mathbf{K}$ is typically found on the surface of good conductors in time-varying fields or in idealized models involving current sheets.
geometric-bending-08111f55.conceptual_definition: This equation is one of the four electromagnetic boundary conditions derived from Maxwell's equations. It is obtained by applying the integral form of the Ampere-Maxwell Law, $\oint \mathbf{H} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = I_{f,enc} + \frac{d\Phi_D}{dt}$, to an infinitesimally thin rectangular loop that straddles the boundary between two media. The result shows that any jump in the tangential component of the $\mathbf{H}$-field is sourced by a free surface current.
geometric-bending-08111f55.intuitive_summary: Imagine a sheet of electric current flowing along a surface. This current sheet creates a 'kink' or a sudden jump in the magnetic field that runs parallel to the surface. The size and direction of this jump are determined precisely by the density and direction of the surface current. If there is no current on the surface, the tangential magnetic field is smooth and continuous as you cross from one side to the other.
geometric-bending-08111f55.description: Relates the discontinuity in the tangential component of the magnetic field intensity ($\mathbf{H}$) across an interface to the free surface current density ($\mathbf{K}$) flowing on that interface.

angular-flux-3187bc85.title: Angular Flux

P.name: Angular Flux
P.description: The power radiated per unit solid angle by an oscillating electric dipole.

\\mu_0.name: Magnetic Permeability of Free Space
\\mu_0.description: A fundamental physical constant that describes the magnetic field generated by electric currents in a vacuum. It is approximately 4\pi \times 10^{-7} N/A^2.

p_0.name: Amplitude of Electric Dipole Moment
p_0.description: The maximum value of the time-varying electric dipole moment of the oscillating source. It represents the strength of the oscillating charge separation.

\\omega.name: Angular Frequency
\\omega.description: The rate at which the electric dipole moment oscillates, measured in radians per second. It is related to the frequency u by \omega = 2\pi u.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The speed at which electromagnetic waves propagate in a vacuum, a fundamental constant of nature, approximately 299,792,458 m/s.

p.name: Linear Momentum ($p$)
p.description: The magnitude of linear momentum, representing the quantity of motion of a particle.

\\pi.name: Pi constant
\\pi.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter (approx. 3.14159).

angular-flux-3187bc85.interpretation: The formula for angular flux, denoted by $P$, is given by $P = \frac{\mu_0 p_0^2 \omega^4}{12\pi c}$. Here, $\mu_0$ is the magnetic permeability of free space, a fundamental constant that describes the magnetic field generated by electric currents. $p_0$ represents the amplitude of the oscillating electric dipole moment, which is a measure of the separation of positive and negative charges and their magnitude, oscillating harmonically. The term $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the oscillation, indicating how rapidly the dipole moment changes. A higher angular frequency leads to a significantly increased radiated power, as indicated by the $\omega^4$ dependence. Finally, $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, a universal constant that governs the propagation of electromagnetic waves. The formula shows that the angular flux is directly proportional to the square of the dipole moment amplitude and the fourth power of the angular frequency, while it is inversely proportional to the speed of light. The constant $\frac{1}{12\pi}$ arises from the integration over all solid angles for a dipole radiating in three dimensions.
angular-flux-3187bc85.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the Larmor formula for radiation from accelerating charges, specifically adapted for an oscillating electric dipole. The derivation involves calculating the electromagnetic fields produced by a time-varying dipole moment and then computing the Poynting vector, which represents the energy flux. Integration of the Poynting vector over a large sphere and averaging over a full oscillation cycle yields the total radiated power. The angular distribution of this power is then obtained by considering the Poynting vector's directional component.
angular-flux-3187bc85.limits_and_boundary: As the angular frequency $\omega$ approaches zero (i.e., the dipole is not oscillating or oscillating very slowly), the angular flux $P$ approaches zero, indicating no radiation. As the angular frequency $\omega$ approaches infinity, the angular flux $P$ approaches infinity, suggesting that very high-frequency oscillations lead to extremely high radiation intensity. If the dipole moment amplitude $p_0$ is zero, then the angular flux $P$ is also zero, as there is no oscillating dipole to generate radiation.
angular-flux-3187bc85.conceptual_definition: The formula for angular flux quantifies the total power radiated by an oscillating electric dipole into a unit solid angle. This represents the directional intensity of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a source whose charge distribution varies harmonically in time. Specifically, it describes the power per unit solid angle emitted in a particular direction, which is crucial for understanding the spatial distribution of radiated energy.
angular-flux-3187bc85.intuitive_summary: Angular flux is the directional power radiated by an oscillating electric dipole, proportional to the square of its dipole moment, the fourth power of its oscillation frequency, and inversely proportional to the speed of light.

infinite-stretch-89801897.title: Geodesic Deviation Equation (Tidal Acceleration Form)

\\frac{D^2}{d\\tau^2}.name: Second Covariant Derivative with respect to Proper Time
\\frac{D^2}{d\\tau^2}.description: An operator that calculates the rate of change of a vector's rate of change along a curve in a way that is independent of the coordinate system.

\\xi^\\mu.name: Geodesic Separation Vector
\\xi^\\mu.description: An infinitesimal vector connecting two nearby geodesics at the same proper time.

\\tau.name: Proper Time
\\tau.description: The time measured by a clock moving along a specific geodesic.

R^\\mu_{\\nu\\rho\\sigma}.name: Riemann Curvature Tensor
R^\\mu_{\\nu\\rho\\sigma}.description: A tensor that encodes the curvature of spacetime. It quantifies the extent to which the covariant derivative fails to commute.

U^\\nu.name: Four-velocity
U^\\nu.description: A four-vector representing the velocity of a particle in spacetime. Its components are derivatives of the spacetime coordinates with respect to proper time.

\\mu,\\nu,\\rho,\\sigma.name: Spacetime Indices
\\mu,\\nu,\\rho,\\sigma.description: Indices ranging from 0 to 3, representing the time and three spatial dimensions in abstract index notation.

infinite-stretch-89801897.symmetry_origin: General Covariance (Diffeomorphism Invariance). The equation is derived by applying the principle of equivalence to a pair of nearby test particles, whose individual paths are governed by the geodesic equation. The Riemann tensor $R^\mu_{\nu\rho\sigma}$ is the fundamental coordinate-invariant object capturing local spacetime curvature.
infinite-stretch-89801897.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of flat spacetime, the Riemann curvature tensor $R^\mu_{\nu\rho\sigma}$ vanishes, causing the right-hand side to become zero. The equation simplifies to $\frac{D^2 \xi^\mu}{d\tau^2} = 0$, indicating that nearby geodesics remain parallel and their separation vector changes at a constant rate, recovering the principle of inertia in special relativity.
infinite-stretch-89801897.conceptual_definition: The geodesic deviation equation states that the tidal acceleration, represented by the second covariant derivative of the separation vector $\xi^\mu$ with respect to proper time $\tau$, $\frac{D^2 \xi^\mu}{d\tau^2}$, is determined by the action of the Riemann curvature tensor $R^\mu_{\nu\rho\sigma}$ on the four-velocity $U$ of the reference geodesic and the separation vector $\xi$ itself. It is the fundamental equation describing how spacetime curvature manifests as tidal forces.
infinite-stretch-89801897.intuitive_summary: Imagine two dust particles floating freely in space near a star. Although both are in 'free fall', the one closer to the star is pulled slightly more strongly. This equation precisely calculates their growing separation (or convergence), revealing that what we perceive as a 'tidal force' is actually the geometry of spacetime being curved by the star's mass.
infinite-stretch-89801897.description: This equation, also known as the Jacobi equation, quantifies the relative acceleration between two nearby geodesics, expressing the tidal force in General Relativity as a function of spacetime curvature.

neutrino-clock-8564e89f.title: Entropy Density of a Relativistic Gas (Natural Units)

s.name: Entropy Density
s.description: The amount of thermodynamic entropy per unit volume.

g_*.name: Effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom
g_*.description: A weighted sum of the number of internal degrees of freedom for all particle species that are relativistic at temperature T.

T.name: Temperature
T.description: The absolute temperature of the relativistic particle gas.

neutrino-clock-8564e89f.interpretation: This equation is a simplified form of the cosmological entropy density, expressed in natural units ($k_B = \hbar = c = 1$). Here, $s$ represents the entropy density, with SI units of Joules per Kelvin per cubic meter (J K⁻¹ m⁻³). The term $g_*$ is the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom, a dimensionless quantity that sums the contributions from all particles for which the thermal energy $k_B T$ is much greater than their rest mass energy $mc^2$. It is calculated as $g_* = \sum_{i=\text{bosons}} g_i + \frac{7}{8} \sum_{j=\text{fermions}} g_j$, where $g_i$ and $g_j$ are the internal degrees of freedom (e.g., spin states) for each particle species. The factor of $7/8$ for fermions arises from the difference between Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein statistics. $T$ is the absolute temperature of the thermal bath. The numerical prefactor $\frac{2\pi^2}{45}$ is a constant derived from the integration of the phase space distribution for relativistic bosons. The formula is crucial for tracking the thermal history of the universe, as the total entropy in a comoving volume, $S = s a^3$ (where $a$ is the scale factor), is conserved under most conditions.
neutrino-clock-8564e89f.symmetry_origin: The formula is derived from the principles of statistical mechanics applied to a system in thermal equilibrium. This equilibrium state is a state of maximum entropy, consistent with the Second Law of Thermodynamics. The derivation relies on the fundamental symmetries of an isotropic and homogeneous universe (the Cosmological Principle), which allows for the definition of a global temperature $T$. It also implicitly uses the permutation symmetry of identical particles, which leads to the Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac distributions that are integrated to obtain this result.
neutrino-clock-8564e89f.limits_and_boundary: This formula is valid in the relativistic limit, where the thermal energy $k_B T$ is much larger than the rest mass energies $m c^2$ of the particles contributing to $g_*$. As the temperature $T$ drops below a particle's mass threshold ($k_B T \ll mc^2$), that particle becomes non-relativistic and its contribution to $g_*$ ceases, causing $g_*$ to decrease in discrete steps. In the limit $T \to 0$, the entropy density $s \to 0$, in accordance with the Third Law of Thermodynamics (Nernst's theorem). The formula assumes the particles are in thermal equilibrium and interact weakly.
neutrino-clock-8564e89f.conceptual_definition: In cosmology and statistical physics, the entropy density, $s$, of a system of relativistic particles in thermal equilibrium is a measure of the disorder per unit volume. This formula shows that $s$ is directly proportional to the cube of the temperature, $T^3$, and a factor $g_*$ which counts the effective number of relativistic particle species. This equation is typically expressed in natural units where the Boltzmann constant $k_B$, the reduced Planck constant $\hbar$, and the speed of light $c$ are set to 1.
neutrino-clock-8564e89f.intuitive_summary: Imagine the early universe as a hot, dense soup of fundamental particles. The entropy density measures how much 'disorder' or 'information' is packed into a given volume of this soup. This formula reveals that as the universe expands and cools, the disorder per volume drops very rapidly, proportional to the temperature cubed.
neutrino-clock-8564e89f.description: This formula quantifies the entropy density of a thermal bath of relativistic particles, such as in the early universe, relating it to temperature and the effective number of particle degrees of freedom in a system of natural units.

rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.title: Invariant Mass from Energy-Momentum Relation

m.name: Invariant Mass
m.description: The mass of an object in its own rest frame; a Lorentz-invariant scalar.

c.name: Speed of Light
c.description: The speed of light in a vacuum, a universal physical constant.

E.name: Total Relativistic Energy
E.description: The total energy of a system, including both rest mass energy and kinetic energy.

p.name: Relativistic Momentum
p.description: The magnitude of the momentum of a system, which depends on its velocity relative to the observer.

rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.interpretation: In the equation $m = \frac{1}{c^2} \sqrt{E^2 - p^2 c^2}$, the term $m$ represents the invariant mass, a Lorentz scalar whose value is identical for all observers in uniform motion. The variable $E$ denotes the total relativistic energy of the particle or system, which includes both its rest energy and its kinetic energy. The variable $p$ signifies the magnitude of the total relativistic momentum. The constant $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum. The expression under the square root, $E^2 - p^2 c^2$, is itself a Lorentz invariant quantity equal to $(mc^2)^2$. In the special case of the object's rest frame, where momentum $p=0$, the equation simplifies to $m = E_{rest}/c^2$, which is the famous mass-energy equivalence relation $E_{rest} = mc^2$.
rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.symmetry_origin: The energy-momentum relation is a direct consequence of the symmetries of Minkowski spacetime, described by the Poincaré group. The invariance of the spacetime interval under Lorentz transformations leads to the invariance of the four-momentum's magnitude, $p_\mu p^\mu = -m^2c^2$, from which this formula is derived.
rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.limits_and_boundary: In the rest frame limit where momentum $p \to 0$, the formula simplifies to $m = E_{rest}/c^2$. In the ultra-relativistic or massless limit where $m \to 0$, the relation becomes $E = pc$, which correctly describes massless particles like photons. For classical speeds ($v \ll c$), the kinetic energy is much smaller than the rest energy, and this relativistic formula remains valid, though less practical than classical approximations.
rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.conceptual_definition: The invariant mass, $m$, of a particle or system is a fundamental property that remains constant in all inertial reference frames. It is defined by rearranging the energy-momentum relation, $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$, to solve for $m$. This quantity represents the mass of the object when measured in its own rest frame, where its total momentum is zero.
rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.intuitive_summary: An object's total energy is a composite of its 'motion energy' (kinetic) and its 'existence energy' (rest mass). The invariant mass, $m$, is the fundamental 'existence energy' component that remains after mathematically accounting for the energy of motion. It is the object's true, unchanging mass, independent of its speed.
rest-frame-weight-34ed0ea1.description: This equation defines the invariant mass of an object or system as a Lorentz-invariant quantity derived from its total relativistic energy and momentum, forming a cornerstone of special relativity.

flux-phase-identity-4479f210.title: Aharonov-Bohm Flux-Phase Identity

\\Delta \\phi.name: Phase Difference
\\Delta \\phi.description: The difference in the quantum mechanical phase of a particle's wavefunction between two paths.

q.name: Electric Charge
q.description: The electric charge of the particle acquiring the phase shift.

\\Phi_B.name: Magnetic Flux
\\Phi_B.description: The total magnetic flux enclosed by the particle's path, defined as $\int \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}$.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck Constant
\\hbar.description: The Planck constant divided by $2\pi$, a fundamental constant in quantum mechanics.

flux-phase-identity-4479f210.interpretation: In the equation $\Delta \phi = q \Phi_B / \hbar$, the term $\Delta \phi$ represents the gauge-invariant phase difference acquired by a charged particle's wavefunction after traversing a closed path. This phase shift is directly proportional to the particle's electric charge $q$ and the total magnetic flux $\Phi_B$ passing through the area enclosed by the path. The constant of proportionality is the inverse of the reduced Planck constant, $\hbar$. This relationship is profound because it implies that the particle's behavior is affected by the magnetic field in a region it never enters, a non-local quantum effect mediated by the vector potential. The observability of this phase shift through interference experiments confirms the physical reality of the vector potential beyond its role in classical electromagnetism.
flux-phase-identity-4479f210.symmetry_origin: This identity is a direct consequence of local $U(1)$ gauge invariance in quantum electrodynamics. The phase of a charged particle's wavefunction can be transformed locally, $\psi \to e^{iq\Lambda/\hbar}\psi$, provided the electromagnetic potentials are also transformed. The quantity $\oint \mathbf{A} \cdot d\mathbf{l}$, which equals the magnetic flux $\Phi_B$, is a gauge-invariant observable that emerges from this symmetry structure.
flux-phase-identity-4479f210.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit, as $\hbar \to 0$, the phase $\Delta \phi$ becomes infinitely large (or rapidly oscillating). In the path integral formulation, this rapid oscillation causes destructive interference for all paths, washing out the quantum effect and recovering classical mechanics where the particle is unaffected by fields it does not directly experience. If the charge $q \to 0$ or the magnetic flux $\Phi_B \to 0$, the phase shift $\Delta \phi$ correctly goes to zero, and no interference is observed.
flux-phase-identity-4479f210.conceptual_definition: The Aharonov-Bohm effect demonstrates that the magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ is a physically significant quantity, not just a mathematical convenience. The phase difference $\Delta \phi$ acquired by a charged particle moving along a closed loop is directly proportional to the magnetic flux $\Phi_B$ enclosed by that loop. This phase shift is a purely quantum mechanical phenomenon, vanishing in the classical limit as $\hbar \to 0$.
flux-phase-identity-4479f210.intuitive_summary: Imagine two paths for a quantum particle that go around a magnetic field. Even if the particle never touches the field, the 'potential' for the field (the vector potential) exists everywhere. This potential alters the particle's quantum phase, causing the two paths to interfere with each other differently than if the field were absent. The total phase difference depends on the total magnetic flux 'trapped' between the paths.
flux-phase-identity-4479f210.description: This identity quantifies the quantum mechanical phase shift acquired by a charged particle's wavefunction when it encircles a region of magnetic flux, even if it never passes through the magnetic field itself.

method-of-images-e1a26b80.title: Method of Images
method-of-images-e1a26b80.description: Calculates the electrostatic potential using the Green's function integral representation and equivalent fictitious image charge distributions.

V(\\mathbf{r}).name: Electric Potential
V(\\mathbf{r}).description: The electrostatic potential at observation point $\mathbf{r}$.

\\mathbf{r}.name: Observation Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}.description: The position vector where the electrostatic potential is evaluated.

\\rho(\\mathbf{r}').name: Source Charge Density
\\rho(\\mathbf{r}').description: The continuous charge distribution at source coordinate $\mathbf{r}'$.

\\mathbf{r}'.name: Source Position Vector
\\mathbf{r}'.description: The coordinate vector of the source charge distribution.

G(\\mathbf{r}, \\mathbf{r}').name: Green's Function
G(\\mathbf{r}, \\mathbf{r}').description: The Dirichlet Green's function satisfying the boundary conditions of the electrostatic domain.

d\\tau'.name: Source Volume Element
d\\tau'.description: The infinitesimal volume element of integration over the source domain.

method-of-images-e1a26b80.interpretation: The equation $V(\mathbf{r}) = \int \rho(\mathbf{r}') G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') d\tau'$ expresses the electrostatic potential $V$ at observation point $\mathbf{r}$ arising from a continuous charge density $\rho(\mathbf{r}')$ integrated over volume element $d\tau'$. The kernel $G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}')$ is the Dirichlet Green's function, encapsulating the electrostatic impulse response of a unit point source while satisfying boundary conditions on conducting surfaces. Under the Method of Images, the complex boundary is replaced by equivalent fictitious image charges in an unbounded domain, reducing the Green's function calculation to a superposition of elementary Coulomb potentials.
method-of-images-e1a26b80.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the uniqueness theorems of Laplace's and Poisson's equations, where boundary value solutions are uniquely specified by Dirichlet boundary conditions. Geometric symmetries (planar, spherical, or cylindrical) allow mirror image charges to reproduce surface equipotentials identically.
method-of-images-e1a26b80.limits_and_boundary: As the distance $|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'| \to \infty$, the Green's function approaches the free-space potential $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 |\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}'|}$, recovering the standard multipole potential of localized charge distributions.
method-of-images-e1a26b80.conceptual_definition: The Method of Images is an analytical technique in electrostatics that solves Poisson's equation $\nabla^2 V = -\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$ subject to conducting boundary conditions by substituting the physical boundary with strategic fictitious 'image' charges outside the region of interest. The integral $V(\mathbf{r}) = \int \rho(\mathbf{r}') G(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') d\tau'$ represents the general potential solution in terms of the domain Green's function.
method-of-images-e1a26b80.intuitive_summary: The Method of Images simplifies boundary-value electrostatic problems by replacing physical conducting boundaries with fictitious mirror charges that identically reproduce the boundary conditions.

baseline-rule-8a2afe94.title: Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia)

\\mathbf{F}_{net}.name: Net Force
\\mathbf{F}_{net}.description: The vector sum of all external forces acting on an object.

\\mathbf{v}.name: Velocity
\\mathbf{v}.description: The vector representing the rate of change of an object's position with respect to a frame of reference.

\\text{const}.name: Constant
\\text{const}.description: Indicates that a quantity does not change with respect to time.

\\implies.name: Implies
\\implies.description: A logical operator indicating that if the preceding statement is true, the following statement must also be true.

baseline-rule-8a2afe94.interpretation: The formula $\mathbf{F}_{net} = 0 \implies \mathbf{v} = \text{const}$ is a foundational statement in classical mechanics. The term $\mathbf{F}_{net}$ represents the vector sum of all external forces acting on a body. The condition $\mathbf{F}_{net} = 0$ signifies a state of mechanical equilibrium, where all forces are perfectly balanced. The logical implication $\implies$ means that this condition necessitates the conclusion that follows. The term $\mathbf{v}$ is the velocity vector of the object's center of mass. The statement $\mathbf{v} = \text{const}$ asserts that this velocity vector is constant over time. A constant vector implies that both its magnitude (speed) and its direction are unchanging. This includes the state of rest, where $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, as a special case.
baseline-rule-8a2afe94.symmetry_origin: Invariance of physical laws under spatial translation (Homogeneity of Space). By Noether's theorem, this symmetry implies the conservation of momentum. Newton's First Law is the expression of momentum conservation in the absence of net external forces.
baseline-rule-8a2afe94.limits_and_boundary: This law defines an inertial reference frame and is a cornerstone of classical mechanics. It breaks down in non-inertial (accelerating) frames, where fictitious forces must be introduced to explain motion. In the relativistic limit ($v \to c$), the law holds, but momentum is redefined as $\mathbf{p} = \gamma m_0 \mathbf{v}$. In the quantum limit (the classical limit is $\hbar \to 0$), a free particle with definite momentum is described by a delocalized plane wave, and the classical concept of a precise trajectory is replaced by probabilistic quantum mechanics.
baseline-rule-8a2afe94.conceptual_definition: In an inertial frame of reference, an object either remains at rest or continues to move at a constant velocity, unless acted upon by a net external force. This principle establishes the concept of inertia, the resistance of any physical object to any change in its state of motion, and defines the set of reference frames (inertial frames) in which Newton's laws of motion hold.
baseline-rule-8a2afe94.intuitive_summary: An object 'wants' to keep doing what it's already doing. If it's sitting still, it stays still. If it's moving, it keeps moving in the same direction and at the same speed, unless an unbalanced push or pull acts on it.
baseline-rule-8a2afe94.description: Newton's First Law of Motion, the law of inertia, states that an object's velocity remains constant unless acted upon by a non-zero net external force.

causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.interpretation: The equation defines the causal propagator $\Delta(x-y)$ as an integral over all possible three-momenta $\mathbf{k}$. The product $k(x-y)$ in the exponent is the Lorentz scalar product $k_\mu (x^\mu - y^\mu)$. The term $\frac{d^3k}{(2\pi)^3 2\omega_k}$ is the Lorentz-invariant measure for integration over the positive-energy mass shell in momentum space. The energy $\omega_k$ is given by the relativistic dispersion relation $\omega_k = \sqrt{|\mathbf{k}|^2c^2 + m^2c^4}/\hbar$. The term $e^{-ik(x-y)}$ represents a positive-frequency plane wave propagating from spacetime point $y$ to $x$, while $e^{ik(x-y)}$ represents a negative-frequency wave. The subtraction ensures the result is zero for spacelike separations (when $(x-y)^2 < 0$), which is the mathematical statement of microcausality.
causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.symmetry_origin: The structure of the propagator is a direct consequence of Lorentz invariance and the canonical commutation relations of quantum field theory. Lorentz invariance demands that the function depends only on the spacetime interval $(x-y)^2$, while the commutation relations enforce that the commutator vanishes for spacelike separations, upholding microcausality.
causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.limits_and_boundary: The defining boundary condition is that $\Delta(x-y) = 0$ for any spacelike separation, i.e., when $(x-y)^2 < 0$. For timelike separations, the propagator is non-zero. In the massless limit ($m \to 0$), the propagator is non-zero only on the light cone, becoming proportional to $\delta((x-y)^2)\text{sgn}(x^0-y^0)$, where $\text{sgn}$ is the sign function.
causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.conceptual_definition: The causal propagator, $i\Delta(x-y)$, is defined as the vacuum expectation value of the commutator of two free scalar field operators, $\langle 0 | [\hat{\phi}(x), \hat{\phi}(y)] | 0 \rangle$. Its integral representation is a superposition of all possible momentum modes, constructed such that the propagation amplitude is zero unless the spacetime interval $(x-y)^2$ is timelike or lightlike, respecting the principle of causality.
causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.intuitive_summary: Imagine sending a ripple through a quantum field from point A to point B. The causal propagator tells you the net effect of this disturbance. It's cleverly built to be exactly zero if a light signal couldn't travel between A and B, ensuring that effects don't travel faster than light. It's the field's way of enforcing the universe's ultimate speed limit.
causal-propagator-6b4b6a9b.description: Defines the Pauli-Jordan function, or causal propagator, for a free scalar field as the vacuum expectation value of the field commutator. It is a Lorentz-invariant Green's function that vanishes for spacelike separations, enforcing microcausality.

scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.title: Klein-Gordon Equation for a Free Scalar Field

\\phi.name: Scalar Field
\\phi.description: A field that assigns a single scalar value to each point in spacetime, representing a spin-0 particle.

m.name: Mass
m.description: The rest mass of the particle quantum associated with the scalar field $\phi$.

\\Box.name: d'Alembert Operator
\\Box.description: The Lorentz-invariant spacetime Laplacian operator, defined as $\Box \equiv \partial_\mu \partial^\mu = \frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} - \nabla^2$.

scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.interpretation: The equation $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$ relates the dynamics of a scalar field $\phi$ to its intrinsic mass $m$. The term $\phi = \phi(x^\mu)$ represents the scalar field, a physical quantity that has a magnitude but no direction at every point in spacetime $x^\mu$; it is the quantum mechanical wave function for a spin-0 particle. The operator $\Box$ is the d'Alembert operator, defined as $\Box = \partial_\mu \partial^\mu = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} - \nabla^2$, where $c$ is the speed of light, $t$ is time, and $\nabla^2$ is the Laplacian operator. The term $m$ represents the rest mass of the particle described by the field $\phi$. The equation is a linear, homogeneous partial differential equation whose solutions describe the propagation of free scalar particles like the Higgs boson.
scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.symmetry_origin: The Klein-Gordon equation is derived by applying the Euler-Lagrange equations of motion to the Lagrangian density for a free scalar field, $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}(\partial_\mu \phi)(\partial^\mu \phi) - \frac{1}{2}m^2\phi^2$. This Lagrangian is constructed to be invariant under transformations of the Poincaré group (spacetime translations, rotations, and Lorentz boosts), ensuring the resulting physics is consistent with special relativity.
scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.limits_and_boundary: In the massless limit where $m \to 0$, the equation simplifies to the homogeneous wave equation, $\Box\phi = 0$, which describes a scalar particle propagating at the speed of light $c$. In the non-relativistic limit, where particle velocities are much less than $c$, the Klein-Gordon equation can be shown to approximate the Schrödinger equation for a free particle. As a quantum field equation, it is fundamentally incompatible with the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$ without further interpretation, as the field $\phi$ itself is a quantum object.
scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.conceptual_definition: The Klein-Gordon equation, $(\Box + m^2)\phi = 0$, is the equation of motion for a free scalar field $\phi$. It is a relativistic generalization of the Schrödinger equation and dictates that the spacetime curvature of the field, represented by the d'Alembertian operator $\Box$, is directly proportional to the field's value, with the constant of proportionality being the negative square of the particle's mass $m$. This describes the propagation of a massive, spin-0 particle through spacetime.
scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.intuitive_summary: Imagine spacetime as a medium filled with a substance, the scalar field $\phi$. This equation is the rule for how waves or ripples travel through that substance. The mass term $m$ acts like a 'stiffness' or 'inertia' for the field; a heavier particle's field resists disturbance more, causing its influence to be more localized, while a massless particle's field propagates outward as a wave at the speed of light.
scalar-dynamics-5c602d48.description: A relativistic wave equation in quantum field theory that describes the dynamics of a free (non-interacting) spin-0 particle, known as a scalar boson.

anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.interpretation: In the relation $M = \frac{v}{c_s}$, $M$ represents the dimensionless Mach number, $v$ denotes the magnitude of the local relative flow velocity, and $c_s$ is the local speed of sound determined by the thermodynamic state of the fluid medium via $c_s = \sqrt{(\partial P / \partial \rho)_s}$. For $M < 0.3$, density variations are negligible (incompressible regime); for $M < 1$, the flow is subsonic; at $M = 1$, the flow is sonic; for $M > 1$, supersonic flow develops characteristic shock fronts; and for $M > 5$, hypersonic regime effects dominate.
anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.symmetry_origin: Scale invariance of the compressible Euler and Navier-Stokes equations under kinematic similitude transformations.
anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $v \to 0$ or $c_s \to \infty$, $M \to 0$, recovering the incompressible fluid dynamics limit where acoustic waves propagate quasi-instantaneously across the domain. In the limit $M \gg 1$, pressure disturbances cannot propagate upstream, forming thin hydrodynamic shocks governed by the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions.
anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.conceptual_definition: The Mach number $M = \frac{v}{c_s}$ parameterizes the relative importance of fluid advection compared to acoustic wave propagation, governing compressibility effects and flow regime classification.
anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.intuitive_summary: It measures whether a fluid element moves faster than the pressure signals that warn the medium ahead of its approach.
anti-newtonian-be7d6bde.description: Defines the Mach number as the dimensionless ratio of local flow velocity to the local acoustic wave propagation speed.

dust-model-3386642e.title: Cosmological Dust Matter Density Scaling

\\rho_m.name: Matter Energy Density
\\rho_m.description: The energy density of non-relativistic matter components in the universe.

a.name: Cosmic Scale Factor
a.description: A dimensionless parameter describing the relative expansion of the universe, normalized to $a=1$ at the present epoch.

\\propto.name: Proportionality Operator
\\propto.description: Indicates that two quantities are directly proportional to each other.

dust-model-3386642e.interpretation: The equation $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$ signifies a direct proportionality between the matter density, denoted by $\rho_m$, and the inverse cube of the cosmic scale factor, $a$. The symbol $\propto$ indicates proportionality. This means that if the cosmic scale factor $a$ doubles, the matter density $\rho_m$ will decrease by a factor of $2^3 = 8$. This relationship arises because, in a uniformly expanding universe, the total amount of matter remains constant, while the volume of space containing that matter increases as $a^3$. Therefore, the density ($\rho_m = \text{Mass/Volume}$) must decrease as the volume increases. This specific scaling applies to matter components that are non-relativistic (their speeds are much less than the speed of light), which is often referred to as 'dust' in cosmological contexts. For relativistic particles like photons or neutrinos, the density scales differently due to their energy losing photons and momentum shifts during expansion.
dust-model-3386642e.symmetry_origin: This scaling law arises from the fundamental principle of mass-energy conservation for non-relativistic particles within a comoving volume in an expanding, homogeneous, and isotropic universe, as described by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric. It is not directly tied to a specific gauge symmetry but rather to the global conservation of matter content under spatial expansion.
dust-model-3386642e.limits_and_boundary: This relationship, $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$, is strictly valid for non-relativistic matter, where particle velocities are much less than the speed of light ($v \ll c$). For relativistic particles, such as photons or highly energetic neutrinos, the energy density scales as $\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$ due to the additional redshift of particle momenta (energy loss) as the universe expands. At very early times in the universe's history, when $a$ was very small, matter density was extremely high. As $a \to \infty$ (the far future), the matter density $\rho_m \to 0$, indicating a highly dilute universe dominated by other components like dark energy.
dust-model-3386642e.conceptual_definition: The cosmological 'dust' model posits that the energy density of non-relativistic matter, denoted by $\rho_m$, decreases proportionally to the inverse cube of the cosmic scale factor, $a$, as the universe expands. This relationship, expressed as $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$, is a direct consequence of the conservation of the total mass of non-relativistic particles within a comoving volume.
dust-model-3386642e.intuitive_summary: Imagine a fixed amount of 'stuff' (like dust particles) spread out in a balloon. As the balloon inflates, the total amount of stuff stays the same, but the volume it occupies grows. Since density is mass divided by volume, the density of the dust must decrease as the balloon gets bigger. In the universe, the 'balloon' is space, and its expansion is measured by the scale factor $a$. The volume grows as $a^3$, so the density of non-relativistic matter (dust) shrinks as $1/a^3$.
dust-model-3386642e.description: This formula describes how the energy density of non-relativistic matter, often referred to as 'dust' in cosmology, scales with the cosmic expansion. It states that the matter density is inversely proportional to the cube of the cosmic scale factor, reflecting the conservation of mass in an expanding volume.

cp-violation-e4cf623d.title: Low-Temperature Electroweak Sphaleron Transition Rate

\\Gamma_{sph}.name: Sphaleron Transition Rate
\\Gamma_{sph}.description: The rate or frequency of electroweak sphaleron transitions, which are non-perturbative processes that violate baryon and lepton number.

M_W.name: W Boson Mass
M_W.description: The mass of the W boson, a fundamental parameter in the electroweak theory, representing a characteristic energy scale.

\\alpha_W.name: Electroweak Coupling Constant
\\alpha_W.description: The effective electroweak coupling constant, related to the strength of the electroweak interaction.

T.description: The temperature of the system, representing the average thermal energy available for particle interactions.

cp-violation-e4cf623d.interpretation: The formula $\Gamma_{sph} \sim e^{-M_W/\alpha_W T}$ describes the approximate rate of electroweak sphaleron transitions. Here, $\Gamma_{sph}$ represents the sphaleron transition rate, which quantifies the frequency of non-perturbative processes that can change baryon and lepton numbers. The term $M_W$ is the mass of the W boson, a fundamental parameter of the electroweak theory, representing a characteristic energy scale. $\alpha_W$ is the electroweak coupling constant, a dimensionless quantity that determines the strength of the electroweak interaction. $T$ is the temperature of the system, representing the average thermal energy available. The ratio $M_W/\alpha_W$ effectively sets the energy scale of the sphaleron barrier, $E_{sph}$, that must be overcome for a transition to occur. The exponential factor $e^{-M_W/\alpha_W T}$ signifies a Boltzmann-like suppression, indicating that transitions are exponentially suppressed when the thermal energy $T$ is much smaller than the energy barrier $M_W/\alpha_W$.
cp-violation-e4cf623d.symmetry_origin: This formula describes the rate of processes (sphaleron transitions) that violate baryon and lepton number conservation, which are accidental global symmetries of the classical Standard Model Lagrangian. These symmetries are explicitly broken at the quantum level by the chiral anomaly. Sphalerons represent saddle points in the electroweak vacuum energy landscape, mediating transitions between topologically distinct vacuum states with different baryon and lepton numbers. The formula quantifies the thermal activation rate over this energy barrier, thus relating to the non-conservation of these symmetries.
cp-violation-e4cf623d.limits_and_boundary: This formula is primarily valid in the low-temperature regime, specifically when $T \ll M_W/\alpha_W$. In this limit, as $T \to 0$, the exponent $-M_W/(\alpha_W T)$ approaches $-\infty$, causing the transition rate $\Gamma_{sph}$ to approach $0$ exponentially. This signifies that sphaleron transitions are highly suppressed at very low temperatures. Conversely, in the high-temperature limit ($T \gg M_W/\alpha_W$), this exponential suppression is overcome, and the formula is no longer accurate; the rate is instead dominated by polynomial terms, such as $\Gamma_{sph} \sim (\alpha_W T)^4$.
cp-violation-e4cf623d.conceptual_definition: The electroweak sphaleron transition rate, $\Gamma_{sph}$, is proportional to an exponential factor $e^{-E_{sph}/T}$, where $E_{sph}$ is the sphaleron energy barrier and $T$ is the temperature. In the low-temperature approximation, $E_{sph}$ is proportional to $M_W/\alpha_W$, leading to the given form.
cp-violation-e4cf623d.intuitive_summary: Imagine a ball trying to roll over a hill. If the hill is very high (large energy barrier) and the ball doesn't have much energy (low temperature), it's very unlikely to get over. This formula shows that the rate of such 'over-the-hill' processes (like sphaleron transitions) drops dramatically as the temperature decreases or the energy barrier increases.
cp-violation-e4cf623d.description: This formula describes the rate of electroweak sphaleron transitions, $\Gamma_{sph}$, in the low-temperature regime, exhibiting an exponential suppression characteristic of thermal activation over an energy barrier.

bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.title: Bragg's Law

d.name: Interplanar Spacing
d.description: The distance between adjacent parallel planes of atoms in a crystal lattice.

\\theta.name: Glancing Angle
\\theta.description: The angle between the incident wave and the scattering planes of the crystal. Also known as the Bragg angle.

n.name: Order of Diffraction
n.description: A positive integer representing the order of the constructive interference maximum.

\\lambda.name: Wavelength
\\lambda.description: The wavelength of the incident radiation (e.g., X-ray, electron, or neutron wave).

bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.interpretation: Bragg's Law, expressed as $2d \sin\theta = n\lambda$, provides the condition for observing a diffraction maximum (constructive interference). The term $2d\sin\theta$ represents the path length difference between two parallel waves scattering from adjacent crystal planes separated by a distance $d$. The angle $\theta$ is the glancing angle, defined as the angle between the incident ray and the scattering plane. For the scattered waves to interfere constructively, this path difference must be an integer multiple of their wavelength $\lambda$. The integer $n$ is the order of the diffraction, where $n=1$ corresponds to the first-order maximum, $n=2$ to the second-order, and so on. This relationship is fundamental to diffraction techniques like X-ray Crystallography (XRD) used to determine the atomic structure of materials.
bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.symmetry_origin: The law is a direct consequence of the discrete translational symmetry of the crystal lattice. The constructive interference condition arises from the coherent superposition of waves scattered from periodically arranged scattering centers (atoms), which is a physical manifestation of this underlying spatial periodicity.
bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.limits_and_boundary: The law imposes a physical limit on diffraction: for an interference maximum of order $n \ge 1$ to be observed, the wavelength $\lambda$ must be no larger than twice the interplanar spacing $d$, i.e., $\lambda \le 2d$. If $\lambda > 2d$, the condition $\sin\theta = n\lambda/(2d) \le 1$ cannot be satisfied. The maximum possible diffraction order is given by $n_{max} = \lfloor 2d/\lambda \rfloor$. The law is derived from classical wave theory and applies to quantum matter waves (e.g., electrons, neutrons) by substituting their de Broglie wavelength for $\lambda$.
bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.conceptual_definition: Bragg's Law specifies the condition for constructive interference from waves (such as X-rays, neutrons, or electrons) scattering from the periodic atomic planes of a crystalline solid. The law states that constructive interference occurs when the total path difference for waves reflecting from adjacent planes, given by the term $2d \sin\theta$, is an integer multiple of the wavelength $\lambda$.
bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.intuitive_summary: Imagine a crystal as a stack of perfectly spaced, semi-transparent mirrors representing atomic planes. Bragg's Law provides the specific angles at which incident waves (like X-rays) will reflect in unison from these layers, creating a strong, bright signal. This pattern of bright spots directly reveals the spacing between the atomic layers.
bragg-s-law-1ba7964c.description: Describes the condition for constructive interference of waves scattered by a crystal lattice, relating the incident wavelength, interplanar spacing, and scattering angle.

photoelectric-law-e38dd99b.title: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation
photoelectric-law-e38dd99b.interpretation:
The equation $K_{max} = h
u - \Phi$ states that the maximum kinetic energy ($K_{max}$) of an emitted electron (photoelectron) is equal to the energy of the incident photon ($h
u$) minus the work function ($\Phi$) of the material. Here, $h$ is Planck's constant, a fundamental constant of nature that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency. The symbol $
u$ represents the frequency of the incident light, making the term $h
u$ the energy carried by a single photon. The work function, $\Phi$, is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of the material; this energy is a characteristic property of the material itself. Therefore, if the photon's energy $h
u$ is less than $\Phi$, no electron will be emitted. If $h
u$ is greater than $\Phi$, the excess energy, $h
u - \Phi$, is converted into the kinetic energy of the emitted electron. $K_{max}$ represents the upper limit of this kinetic energy because some electrons may lose additional energy through internal collisions before escaping the material.
photoelectric-law-e38dd99b.symmetry_origin: The equation is a direct consequence of the conservation of energy, which, by Noether's theorem, arises from the time-translation symmetry of the physical laws governing the system.
photoelectric-law-e38dd99b.limits_and_boundary:
This equation is non-relativistic and applies to electrons ejected at speeds $v \ll c$. For photoelectrons with speeds approaching the speed of light, the kinetic energy term $K_{max}$ must be replaced by the relativistic expression $(\gamma - 1)m_e c^2$. In the classical limit where Planck's constant $h 	o 0$, the photon energy vanishes, and this quantum effect cannot be explained. A critical boundary condition is the threshold frequency $
u_0 = \Phi/h$; for incident frequencies $
u < 
u_0$, the photon energy is insufficient to overcome the work function, and no photoemission occurs, meaning $K_{max}$ is undefined or zero.

\\nu.name: Photon Frequency
